name: Cheese affinage (ripeness judged by touch)
open_problem: An affineur decides when a wheel of cheese is at peak maturity by pressing it with the fingertips and using accumulated sensory instinct; there is no objective, non-destructive instrument that predicts optimal ripeness per-wheel, so timing-to-market is done by feel.
verbatim_quote: The skilled affineur will need to use their finely-tuned senses (alongside a grading iron) to ascertain the cheese's stage of maturity and make decisions as to whether the cheese is ready for market.

name: Koji (Aspergillus) cultivation timing by smell/feel
open_problem: Koji makers judge when mold growth on rice/beans is finished by looking at the mycelia and smelling/tasting for a fruity-floral note; this finicky tacit skill is passed hand-to-hand and has no reliable in-tray sensor for end-point detection.
verbatim_quote: Sake craftspeople oversee the process to ensure the mould grows in optimal conditions by adjusting temperature and humidity, and their work determines the quality of the sake.

name: Soy sauce / miso moromi maturity assessment
open_problem: Maturity of the moromi (fermenting mash) over 6-18+ months is still gauged by an experienced brewer's nose and eye; the literature itself notes the lack of any objective, fast, intuitive maturity metric.
verbatim_quote: there is currently a deficiency of an objective, fast, and intuitive evaluation method for maturity.

name: Dry-cured ham testing by the 'cala' (bone-needle smell test)
open_problem: Whether a 24-36 month jamon is correctly cured is verified by a 'calador' who pierces the ham at four points with a bone spike and judges the released aroma; the entire quality gate depends on one expert's trained sense of smell with no instrument substitute.
verbatim_quote: The 'cala' is a very complex process and it is necessary to have an excellent and highly developed sense of smell developed through experience.

name: Sourdough bulk-fermentation / proof end-point ('poke test')
open_problem: Bakers ignore the clock and decide dough is proofed by how it looks and springs back to a finger poke; end-point depends on temperature and starter vigor and is learned by watching the dough, with no consumer-accessible objective readiness signal.
verbatim_quote: Use time as a guideline, but let the dough tell you when it's ready.

name: Wine harvest timing (post-veraison ripeness call)
open_problem: The pick date 30-70 days after veraison is a judgment blending lab Brix/pH with tasting seeds and skins; picking a day early or late shifts the wine, and the final call remains a stylistic sensory decision.
verbatim_quote: harvest typically follows 30 to 70 days after véraison, depending on variety, climate, and the winemaker's stylistic goals.

name: Traditional balsamic vinegar barrel maturation
open_problem: Over 12-25 years of annual barrel transfers in an acetaia, the maestro decides which barrel/vintage is ready purely by tasting; each acetaia's progression is idiosyncratic and assessment is by master palate, not measurement.
verbatim_quote: As master tasters know well, each balsamic vinegar is unique and releases an inimitable range of flavours and aromatic notes.

name: Blacksmithing / forge welding heat judged by color
open_problem: Smiths bring steel to forge-welding heat by reading the incandescent color of the metal by eye; the exact temperature is judged visually and learned per-forge, complicated by ambient light, with no affordable real-time guidance.
verbatim_quote: The exact temperature is almost always judged by eye and learned by experience on your set of equipment.

name: Pottery kiln firing without instruments
open_problem: Traditional potters control temperature, soak time and oxidation/reduction atmosphere by reading flame color, ember glow and the look of the pots; this is instinctive expert knowledge with no low-cost sensing of in-kiln atmosphere/temperature for the artisan.
verbatim_quote: Without pyrometers or electric kilns, traditional potters relied on the color of the flames, the glowing embers, and the appearance of the pots themselves to gauge temperature, duration, and atmosphere parameters.

name: Glassblowing (working glass at the right viscosity by eye)
open_problem: A gaffer keeps molten glass in the narrow workable viscosity band by reading its color (e.g. bright orange near 1090 C) and feel, knowing when to reheat; it is kinesthetic memory built over years with no instrument feeding the working state in real time.
verbatim_quote: The working temperature is reduced in the furnace to around 1,090 °C (2,000 °F), at which stage the glass appears to be a bright orange color.

name: Handloom weaving warp-tension management by feel
open_problem: On traditional shuttle looms the weaver continuously feels warp tension, reads the cloth and adjusts by hand for hours; even tension across hundreds of threads is maintained purely by tactile judgment with no assistive feedback.
verbatim_quote: Traditional shuttle looms depend entirely on human judgment, and they require a weaver who can feel the tension, read the cloth, and respond to the material as it behaves under their hands.

name: Dry stone walling (stone selection and fit by eye)
open_problem: A mortarless wall stands only by gravity, friction and the waller's eye for which irregular stone to place where; certification is a timed hands-on rebuild, and stone selection/placement is an un-tooled spatial-reasoning skill judged by experts.
verbatim_quote: Dry stone walling is so durable because it contains no mortar to crack and fail, but is held together merely by the weight of stone, and by the skill of the builder who selected and fitted the stones together.

name: Japanese kumiko / nail-free joinery fitting
open_problem: Kumiko pieces hold together by pressure alone, requiring each thin slat to be planed, sawn and chiseled to a hand-fitted tolerance; achieving the exact interference fit is a by-hand fine-adjustment skill with no digital aid for the artisan.
verbatim_quote: Thinly-slit wooden pieces are grooved, punched, and mortised, and then fitted individually using a plane, saw, chisel, and other tools to make fine-adjustments.

name: Vegetable tanning of leather (recipe and feel by master tanner)
open_problem: A master tanner sets tannin sources, concentrations, temperatures and weeks-to-months timings by judgment to hit a target softness/strength/touch; recipes are secret, hide-by-hide, and tuned by feel rather than by a predictive model.
verbatim_quote: The master tanner creates the ideal blend keeping in mind the result he wants to achieve in terms of softness, strength, colour and touch feeling.
